periods.analysis: Peak TSA/CBP passenger wait time starts this series at 24 minutes, which is yellow against the 20-minute target and tells us the gateway is moving but not yet moving cleanly. The pressure was concentrated in the 17:30-20:15 international arrival bank, especially when the Seaport cruise-transfer coaches and two late widebody arrivals hit the Federal Inspection Services hall together. Queue sensors at Checkpoint C and CBP primary showed that the first 18 minutes were usually manageable; the overrun came when lane changes lagged by one staffing cycle. I read this as an operational watch item, not a structural failure, with the specific watch point being Sunday evening staffing alignment.
periods.recommendations: Keep the Airport Operations Center’s 30-minute queue huddle in place on Thursdays through Sundays, with TSA, CBP, airline station managers, and Harborview Aviation staff using the same flight-bank forecast. Add two flex stanchion configurations at Checkpoint C and the east FIS queue so supervisors can open overflow within 10 minutes rather than waiting for the next passenger wave. Publish a weekly Sunday-arrival heat map and use it to pre-authorize CBP overtime for the top five risk banks.

periods.analysis: The peak wait moved the wrong way to 29 minutes, up 5 minutes from 24, still yellow but now uncomfortably close to red. Holiday travel, wet-weather curb congestion, and the temporary closure of FIS Booths 14-16 for camera and counter-height work all landed in the same quarter. TSA lane throughput held reasonably well in the morning, but CBP secondary referrals and baggage recheck lines backed into the primary hall on three December weekends. The watch item is clear: when Terminal 2 international arrivals exceed 1,250 passengers in a 90-minute window, our recovery playbook is still too slow.
periods.recommendations: Move the FIS booth work to overnight punch-list only until the January bank pattern eases, and require a daily open-booth confirmation from the construction superintendent by 04:30. Extend the curb-to-checkpoint passenger ambassador crew on Fridays, Saturdays, and Sundays so cruise and airport flows do not collide at Door 6. Have Aviation Planning test a revised airline arrival-spacing request for the 18:00-19:30 bank before the spring schedule is finalized.

periods.analysis: The measure turned red at 32 minutes, a 3-minute increase from 29, and I am concerned because passengers experience that as a broken promise at the front door of the city. The root causes were specific and manageable: two automated passport control kiosks were down awaiting vendor parts, CBP staffing bids left the late bank thin, and spring-break departures stacked Checkpoint B before the precheck split was fully staffed. The worst days were not random; they followed late Asia arrivals paired with full domestic departure banks and one elevator outage at FIS Lift F-2. Red does not mean panic, but it does mean the airport needs a tighter command rhythm until the peak is back below 30.
periods.recommendations: Stand up a 60-day Passenger Flow Recovery Cell led by Airport Operations, with named TSA, CBP, airline, custodial, and Landside contacts on the 15:00 and 19:00 calls. Require the kiosk vendor to stage two spare passport-control units on site and close work orders within 24 hours for FIS devices. Reassign Harborview Aviation customer-care staff from low-volume lobby posts to Checkpoint B and the FIS recheck belt during the top ten forecasted peak periods each week.

periods.analysis: The peak wait improved to 29 minutes, down 3 minutes from 32, moving us out of red and back to yellow. That is progress, and it came from disciplined work: kiosk uptime returned above 97 percent, CBP opened the east primary row more consistently, and the checkpoint queue huddle started acting on flight-bank data instead of anecdotes. We are still 9 minutes over the 20-minute target, so I am not declaring victory. The watch item is the Monday and Thursday late-afternoon connection wave, where recheck belts R-3 and R-4 still become the choke point after international arrivals.
periods.recommendations: Keep the Recovery Cell active through the summer schedule, but narrow its focus to the 14 highest-risk weekly banks rather than running a broad daily meeting. Add temporary belt marshals at R-3 and R-4 during Monday and Thursday peaks, with handheld counters reporting 15-minute queue depth to the Airport Operations Center. Ask the airlines to protect minimum connection buffers on itineraries that rely on the FIS recheck path until the wait time is consistently below 25 minutes.

periods.analysis: The measure improved again to 25 minutes, down 4 minutes from 29, which is the best result in this run but still yellow against the 20-minute standard. The summer operation was cleaner because the cruise-transfer arrivals were met outside Door 2, the Checkpoint C lane matrix was pre-set before the evening push, and CBP used the mobile supervisor tablet to redeploy officers faster. Harborview is growing, and a 25-minute peak at this volume shows the team can bend the curve when the playbook is followed. The watch item is Labor Day-style surge recovery: if one widebody is 45 minutes late, the queue can still jump faster than our staffing response.
periods.recommendations: Lock the summer playbook into a standard operating procedure before the winter holiday schedule, including the Door 2 cruise-transfer staging plan and the Checkpoint C pre-set lane matrix. Extend the mobile supervisor tablet rollout to the west FIS row and train two additional CBP liaison staff on the dashboard. Run one tabletop drill with TSA, CBP, Port Police, and the three largest international carriers using a delayed-widebody scenario.

periods.analysis: Peak wait time slipped back to 29 minutes, up 4 minutes from 25, so the yellow condition persisted and the margin we earned in Q3 narrowed. The holiday bank was heavier, but the more useful lesson is operational: the new airline winter schedule put three international arrivals within 22 minutes, and the temporary closure of Recheck Belt R-4 removed our best relief valve. TSA kept the departure queue from spilling into ticketing most days, but CBP primary and recheck were again the pinch points. The watch item for me is schedule compression, because no amount of cheerful signage offsets too many passengers arriving at the same federal bottleneck.
periods.recommendations: Use the Airport Scheduling Committee to press carriers for a 10- to 15-minute spread in the 18:00 international bank where slot flexibility exists. Finish R-4 belt controls testing before the next holiday peak and require a backup manual-feed plan any time a recheck belt is out of service. Keep passenger ambassadors deployed at the FIS exit and domestic recheck split, but pair them with live queue data so they are directing flow rather than simply apologizing for it.

periods.analysis: The peak wait returned to red at 32 minutes, up 3 minutes from 29, repeating the Q1 stress pattern from last year. This time the drivers were a federal staffing cap during the late bank, a software patch that took four e-gates out of service for two evenings, and spring-break passenger volumes arriving earlier than the published seasonal forecast. I am concerned because recurrence tells us the system is still too brittle when one technology or staffing assumption fails. The issue is being managed in real time, but the watch item is resilience: we need a second operating mode that works when e-gates or officer counts are below plan.
periods.recommendations: Activate a Q1 Red Recovery Protocol whenever forecast peak wait exceeds 28 minutes, including pre-cleared overflow queuing, airline arrival notifications, and a named federal liaison on the Airport Operations Center bridge. Require the e-gate vendor to schedule software changes outside the 15:00-22:00 arrival window and provide a rollback technician on site for the first two operating nights. Prepare a manual document-check surge layout for the FIS hall so four failed e-gates do not automatically translate into a red passenger experience.

periods.analysis: The peak wait improved to 28 minutes, down 4 minutes from 32, bringing the measure back to yellow but not yet where Harborview needs it. The Red Recovery Protocol helped: e-gate maintenance moved overnight, overflow queuing was opened earlier, and airlines received better advisories before the late international bank. Still, 28 minutes is 8 minutes over target, and the pattern across two years is that we recover after red but have not yet held the system near green. The watch item for the next quarter is sustainability under growth, especially as the new South Concourse gates add connecting passengers into the same checkpoint and FIS ecosystem.
periods.recommendations: Convert the Red Recovery Protocol into a permanent Peak Flow Standard with trigger levels at 24, 28, and 31 minutes, so yellow gets managed before it becomes red. Fund a summer pilot for two additional contract queue coordinators at Checkpoint C and the FIS recheck split, with performance measured by 15-minute throughput and maximum queue depth. Bring TSA, CBP, and the South Concourse airline users into a monthly capacity review until the peak wait is below 25 minutes for two consecutive quarters.

periods.analysis: Peak passenger wait fell from 28 to 25 minutes. That is progress, but passengers still face a five-minute gap to the 20-minute target as checkpoint and international-arrival demand share limited capacity.
periods.recommendations: Retain peak-flow triggers and review lane staffing with TSA and CBP before the next travel peak.
